A comprehensive analysis of graviton production in various processes, including decays and collisions, is provided in this study. The study also explores the potential for detecting gravitons at the Large Hadron Collider, specifically through the detection of gravitational radiation at the future high-energy collider. The prospects of observing gravitational radiation are a crucial aspect of this research.

The second installment of a series focused on using Gaia's astrometry to measure the mass of T~Eri is presented. This time, we utilize the astrometric data from Gaia to track the orbital path of T~Eri A* around its companion, T~Eri B, over a longer period. This is made possible by combining the astrometric data from Gaia with data from the Hipparcos and Gaia Exoplanet Candidate Solution Program. This allows us to accurately measure the full orbit of T~Eri A* and determine its parallax and proper motion. Additionally, we calculate the astrometric mass of T~Eri A* and its companion, yielding a value of 1.32 ± 0.02 solar masses for the primary star. This is consistent with the mass determined by the astrometric solution of the first paper and is also in line with the mass determined by the spectroscopic method.

This study aims to evaluate the effectiveness of various single-point, two-point, and random crossover methods in conjunction with selection techniques like Wheel, Roulette, and Tournament from the population perspectives. To accomplish this, we examine the performance of these algorithms on a 0/1 Knapsack problem, a widely researched benchmark. Through experiments, we assess the algorithms' computational complexity and convergence rates. The results indicate that Roulette and Tournament methods yield superior solutions, with Roulette yielding the best results in all instances. Additionally, we find that two-point crossover paired with the Roulette wheel achieves the lowest computational time.

This paper examines $L^2$ estimates for a specific class of oscillatory operators that are a combination of three convolutions in two dimensions. These operators have a parameter dependence, similar to those studied in a notable paper by F. Nato (2011). The main aim is to establish the existence of these estimates, which would imply the existence of these estimates for a broader range of operators. The method used involves a change of variables, decomposition, and the application of a previous $L^2$ estimate for a single oscillatory operator.

The T5 model has achieved remarkable success in Natural Language Processing tasks, including masked language modeling and zero-shot applications. Its versatility has enabled itToEnd-to-end neural architecture for several downstream tasks, including Natural Language Inference and Hate Speech detection. This work explores the capabilities of T5 in detecting Hate Speech, leveraging its potential for zero-shot and few-shot learning. By utilizing the HateXPress dataset, we investigate the model's performance in a multi-task setting, where it is fine-tuned on a related task, and its performance in a multi-label scenario. Furthermore, we investigate the impact of customizing T5 on Hate Speech detection by incorporating hate-related examples into its pre-training data. Our results demonstrate the model's ability to achieve high accuracy, with an ensemble model reaching 94.2% accuracy, making it a viable option for resource-constrained environments.

Quantum Monte Carlo methods have shown promising results in solving complex many-body problems, particularly in simulating the behavior of electrons in atoms and molecules. However, these methods have been limited in their application to electron correlation and nuclear effects. This study aims to extend the use of these methods to investigate the impact of electron-electron interactions on the properties of ions with fewer electrons. The researchers have proposed a new approach, which involves using a specific type of potential to accurately describe the behavior of ions with fewer electrons. This approach has been tested using various systems, including the ground state of helium, beryllium, and neon. The results show that the method accurately reproduces the known correlation lengths of these systems, which are characterized by a power-law scaling behavior. The researchers have also investigated the impact of system size and boundary conditions on the correlation properties of these ions, which are found to be consistent with theoretical predictions. This study has also shown that the method accurately predicts the impact of ion size on the correlation properties of nearby ions.

The 2020 US presidential election was marred by allegations of fraud, which were largely disseminated through social media. In this study, we investigate the extent of election deception on Twitter, focusing on claims related to the 2020 election. We developed a dataset, VoterFraud2020, comprising 1,065 allegedly fraudulent claims and their corresponding fact-checking outcomes. Notably, our dataset encompasses both fact-checked claims and associated multimedia content, such as images and videos. We employed a range of fact-checking organizations, which allowed us to explore the impact of bias on our dataset. We also examined the relationship between our dataset and user accounts, identifying notable connections. The VoterFraud2020 dataset serves as a valuable resource for researchers studying the dissemination of election deception on social media.

We show that in a large enough, locally next-to-weak mixing $C^1$ diffeomorphism, an almost every point has a neighborhood where the sequence of its $\beta$-emergent points consists of distinct orbit segments. This result holds for any value of $\beta$ in the interval $(0, \log 2)$, provided the dynamical degree of the diffeomorphism is greater than 1. Our proof relies on combining the distributional properties of real numbers with a generic result on generic diffeomorphisms, as well as the use of the topological entropy.

Recent developments in Bayesian Neural Networks have demonstrated the ability to effectively capture uncertainty in complex decision-making processes. However, these methods often struggle to accurately quantify uncertainty in rare and unusual data points. To overcome this limitation, a novel approach has been proposed, which involves encoding the posterior distribution of latent variables in VAEs to quantify uncertainty in Bayesian Neural Networks. By decoupling the latent variables from the neural network's hidden states, it is possible to obtain a more accurate and informative posterior distribution. The proposed method has been successfully applied to regression tasks and has shown significant improvements in uncertainty quantification, particularly in rare cases. The experimental results indicate that this approach can provide more reliable estimates of uncertainty while maintaining computational efficiency, particularly in high-dimensional data.

A comprehensive analysis of electron transport through a quantum dot linked to electrodes via redox groups, as proposed in the Marcus-Levich-Jortner model, has been conducted. The transport behavior of the system was examined in the context of a strong electron-electron interaction within the redox group and a strong electron-electron interaction between the quantum dot and the electrodes. The electron transfer rate was found to be maximized at optimal parameters for the redox group, and this rate was observed to follow an exponential decay from its peak value. The calculated results were found to be consistent with experimental data obtained from an ensemble average of the electron transfer rates. The calculated average rate, however, was found to be in agreement with the Marcus-Levich-Jortner model predictions. The calculated average rate, as a function of the reorganization energy, also showed an inverted S-shaped curve, and the system was found to transition from the non-adiabatic to the adiabatic regime at a certain optimal reorganization energy value. The calculated average rate, however, was found to be in agreement with the Marcus-Levich-Jortner model predictions in both the non-adiabatic and adiabatic regimes.

This research paper presents a novel trajectory tracking method, which effectively integrates a trajectory generator with a trajectory follower. The trajectory generator and follower were previously optimized for high-speed navigation in an autonomous vehicle, but their individual performance was hindered by limitations in precision and range. The paper introduces an innovative solution, which combines the strengths of both components, leveraging the trajectory generator's ability to produce precise paths and the follower's expertise in real-time control and navigation through uncharted terrain. The trajectory generator uses a high-level planning algorithm to generate optimal paths, which are then refined by the trajectory follower using a nonlinear model predictive control approach. The combined system is capable of producing highly accurate trajectories, which are then executed by the vehicle to achieve optimal navigation. The paper validates the effectiveness of the approach through simulation and real-world testing, highlighting its potential to deliver high-performance navigation while minimizing computational requirements.

A theoretical framework for the thermoelectric effect in large thin films is developed, focusing on the phenomenon of magnon drag within the semi-metal regime. This framework is applied to a thin film of a Heusler alloy, with a specific composition of Au$_{1-x}$Pt$_{x}$P, and analyzed in relation to varying film thicknesses and temperatures. The results indicate that the Seebeck coefficient and electrical resistivity exhibit power-law relationships with film thickness, specifically, $T^{-3/2}$ and $T^{-5/2}$ respectively. Furthermore, it is found that the thermoelectric figure of merit experiences a peak value at an optimal temperature of approximately 100 K. The underlying physical mechanism is also explored.

The Perfect Sum problem, a longstanding challenge in combinatorics, has been the subject of extensive research. Notably, in 1881, a mathematician by the name of de Bruijn proposed an equation that could potentially resolve this issue, though it remains unsolved to this day. Our study focuses on a probabilistic approach to tackle this problem, and we've developed a method to estimate the likelihood of achieving a perfect sum using random numbers. Furthermore, we've created an algorithm based on this probabilistic model, and our initial testing demonstrates its effectiveness in solving the Perfect Sum problem.

This paper presents a method for constructing polynomials of higher orders within finite fields, specifically those of degree $n$ over $q$ where $q$ is an odd prime power, given an existing polynomial of degree $n-1$ over the same field. The approach is based on a recursive process that iteratively utilizes an initial high-order polynomial to create a new high-order polynomial, often achieved through the roots of a quadratic factor within the field. The method is demonstrated through several examples, including scenarios involving Dickson polynomials, multiple initial polynomials, and arbitrary fields characteristics.

This paper introduces a novel approach for analyzing source code through formal methods, utilizing the UPPAAL model checking tool. Our proposed method is demonstrated with two case studies, which showcase its effectiveness in examining source code. Furthermore, we outline the potential for further research in this area and identify several challenges that arise from our novel approach.

A novel imaging technique, employing imaging through scattering of structured light, has been developed. This method, utilizing metamaterials, captures an object's details through analysis of light scattered by a patterned surface. This research proposes an enhanced version of this technique, incorporating a unique patterned surface design that maximizes the acquisition of spatial information. The new method also includes a data compression algorithm, utilizing a matrix called a CS matrix, to reduce data volume, and a reconstruction algorithm, utilizing a sparse matrix called a CS matrix, to retrieve the original image. The research also introduces a data compression method, utilizing a patterned surface design, to further enhance image resolution. The new method, combining both data compression and the unique patterned surface design, is shown to significantly improve image resolution, and the experimental results demonstrate its potential for high-resolution imaging.

Theoretical studies have investigated how high-frequency ions are produced through the interaction of high-intensity, circularly polarized lasers with a helium gas. A three-dimensional simulation of this interaction reveals the presence of distinct resonant frequencies, which are caused by the ac-Stark shifts in the helium atoms. These resonant frequencies result in the creation of high-energy ions. Specifically, the creation of H$^-$ and He$^+$ ions follows a periodic pattern, while the creation of HeH$^+$ ions exhibits irregular fluctuations. Moreover, the laser intensity affects the production of these ions differently, leading to varying dependencies on the laser intensity.

We introduce an innovative approach to image blending that builds upon the initial work of the Linear Image Combination framework. Our method, which we call Linear Image Combination with Semantic Projection (LICS), is a more versatile version of LIC that allows for a seamless transition between images. Lics leverages a neural network to identify semantic structures within images and projects them onto a common plane, making it possible to combine images that were previously impossible to mix using the original framework. Our approach is more efficient and requires less data than previous methods, such as the Local Image Combination (LIC) algorithm, which relies on a complex process involving global feature maps and fine-grained local information.

The patterns of gene expression are crucial for the development of complex phenotypes in multicellular organisms. Although the stochastic nature of gene expression has been observed in individual cells, the connection between these dynamics and long-term phenotypic traits is not yet fully understood. This study uses a computational approach to analyze the time courses of single-cell RNA sequencing data, which reveal unique patterns of gene expression variability. By applying a clustering algorithm to these data, we can identify specific characteristics of gene expression trajectories, including the timing of peak expression, the duration of RNA transcripts, and the rate of gene expression change. Our analysis of single-cell RNA sequencing data from various developmental stages shows that we can accurately extract these characteristics from the data, which are strongly correlated with the expression levels of these genes. Furthermore, we found that the size of the population of cells expressing a particular gene and the duration of RNA transcripts are the most informative features for predicting the expression levels of these genes. This study demonstrates the effectiveness of using single-cell RNA sequencing data for analyzing the dynamics of gene expression and linking these dynamics to the expression levels of these genes.

A significant challenge in deep learning lies in the scarcity of labeled data.  While semi-supervised learning can mitigate this issue by combining labeled and unlabeled data, its full potential remains unexplored.  This paper presents a novel semi-supervised learning approach that utilizes unlabeled data to refine a pre-trained model, then applies it to a series of images captured by a robotic arm during a simulated learning process, effectively simulating real-world data collection.  By leveraging a dataset of images taken by a robotic arm during a simulated learning process, a model is trained to predict the color of an object based on its location, effectively simulating real-world data collection.  This approach is then applied to a series of images taken by a robotic arm during a simulated learning process, effectively simulating real-world data collection. In the field of near-term quantum computing, certain quantum algorithms can be viewed as a type of iterative optimization where smaller components called layers are gradually combined. Research has discovered that, in some cases, these optimization processes reach a plateau and fail to make further progress once they've reached a certain point. A closer examination of how these processes work revealed that they often get stuck in a state of equilibrium when dealing with complex problems. Our study provides a mathematical explanation for this phenomenon and shows that it's a common occurrence across different types of algorithms used for this type of optimization. Furthermore, our research suggests that, in most cases, the plateau point is reached before the components of these algorithms can be optimized effectively for solving specific problems.

Individual re-identification involves determining whether a given record in a database corresponds to a specific record in a known reference database. This process is crucial for verifying personal information and reconciling inconsistent data. Accurate matching of database records is a critical component in various applications, including data integration, mining, and the discovery of hidden connections. In this study, a comprehensive review of existing methods for individual re-identification is provided, covering both traditional and advanced approaches. A new framework for evaluating the performance of these methods is introduced, taking into account factors such as the distribution of data, the level of similarity between records, and the complexity of data structures. Furthermore, a comprehensive analysis of state-of-the-art methods is conducted, highlighting their key characteristics and limitations. Finally, a set of future research directions is outlined, focusing on areas such as the development of efficient indexing techniques, the integration of learning-based approaches, and the handling of complex data.

To advance power system modeling, accurate data is required, but accessing such data is often restricted due to its limited availability and sensitivity. Consequently, researchers rely on data from older, less detailed time series sources, which can be inadequate for modern power system analysis. To address this issue, a new method has been developed that enables the creation of more reliable time series data for system modeling, utilizing data from the 1950s in conjunction with physical laws to generate more detailed data. The method has been successfully tested using data from various countries, including the United States and the United Kingdom, and has been found to produce data that is both accurate and detailed. The method has been found to be particularly effective in generating data that is consistent with modern power systems, and has been found to be robust to various data inputs, making it a reliable tool for researchers. The method has been found to be computationally efficient and has been found to be a reliable source of detailed data for power system modeling, making it a valuable resource for researchers.

This research examines the algorithmic convergence of the modified forward-backward projection method, a method that addresses the generalized variational inequality problem and is characterized by the presence of a Lipschitz continuous mapping. The study considers a scenario where the function and the operator are perturbed by an additive error term and demonstrates the method's robust convergence to the problem's unique solution under the condition that the sum of the resolvent domains' diameters is below one. The presented result is shown to be optimal and extends previous work on the forward-backward splitting method and the Tikhonov regularization method for solving variational inequalities.

A Fuchsian group's isomorphic transformation corresponds to an orthogonal rotation within the hyperbolic plane's PSL_(2,R) structure, which has a direct correlation with the group's order. Specifically, for groups of order 16 or less, the isomorphic transformation can be precisely defined, allowing for a comprehensive understanding of their geodesic crossing patterns.

The first investigation into Lepton flavor violation in the decay of $\Upsilon (3S)$ to electron and muon is conducted. The resulting results are used to establish limitations on the Yukawa coupling of a new, hypothetical vector leptoquark particle. This new discovery leads to stricter constraints on the parameter $f_{V}$ within the framework of R-parity-violating supersymmetry, specifically in the context of the coupling $l_iR$ $H_d$.

The Kagome lattice structure, composed of three interconnected triangles, has been a focal point in the study of flat-band physics for a long time. Despite significant research efforts, flat-band superconductivity has not been achieved in Kagome metals. Our research team has successfully synthesized a new class of flat-band Kagome compounds, Pd$_3$P$_2$(S$_{1-x}$Se$_x$)$_8$, using a high-pressure method. By analyzing the Se $L$-edge X-ray absorption near-edge spectra, we have confirmed the successful incorporation of Se into the compound. Upon high-pressure treatment, the superconducting transition temperature ($T_c$) of Pd$_3$P$_2$S$_8$ increases from 3.2 K to 4.0 K, while the compound Pd$_3$P$_2$Se$_8$ exhibits an even higher $T_c$ of 4.3 K. Our findings indicate that the introduction of Se into the compound leads to an increase in the superconducting transition temperature.

We investigate the recovery of black hole perturbations in Jackiw-Teitelboim gravity, specifically analyzing the return to thermodynamic equilibrium following a small energy injection.  A stochastic model is used to describe the near-Horizon behavior of the black hole, treating the horizon as a dissipative boundary that damps out disturbances.  Under this model, the probability of returning to equilibrium is extremely low for typical energy injections, but it increases with larger energy injections.  In the case of Gaussian energy injections, the probability can be calculated exactly, revealing a complex relationship between the return probability and the distribution's variance, specifically a power-law decline for certain parameters and a Cauchy-like behavior for others.

Recent studies have shown that neural ordinary differential equations (ODEs) can efficiently process sequential data and outperform traditional recurrent neural networks. However, these models often rely on continuous data, whereas real-world sequential data is frequently noisy, irregularly sampled, and even sparse. This paper introduces a novel neural ODE framework capable of accommodating noisy, irregularly sampled, and even sparse data, and demonstrates its ability to effectively handle various scenarios. Through experiments on time-series and video data, the framework is shown to be robust against data irregularities and even improve its performance as a result. Additionally, the framework is successfully applied to pose estimation in videos, a task that has garnered significant interest in the field of computer vision.

Recent breakthroughs in vision-language models have enabled the creation of 
agents capable of navigating in simulated environments based on natural language 
instructions. However, existing models often struggle to navigate in novel scenes 
with new language descriptions, largely due to a lack of understanding of visual 
object relationships. To address this limitation, we introduce a new 
vision-language navigation model that leverages a transformer architecture to 
learn and retain visual object information. This information is then used to 
generate a memory-driven plan that guides the agent towards the desired goal. 
Our proposed model has been successfully tested in various environments and 
demonstrates significant improvements over existing models in terms of both 
efficiency and success rates.

Significant advancements in few-shot learning for NLP tasks have been achieved through the application of large language models (LLMs) that can be fine-tuned with minimal data. However, the effectiveness of LLMs heavily relies on the availability of labeled data for specific tasks. This limitation can be overcome by developing models that can learn from task-specific instructions without requiring extensive fine-tuning. Our research presents OPT-IML, a meta-learning framework that enables large language models to learn from task instructions without relying on specific task labels. OPT-IML builds upon the Transformer-XL architecture, allowing it to be applied across various NLP tasks. Our experiments demonstrate that OPT-IML outperforms existing models in both few-shot and zero-shot settings, achieving notable improvements of 2.5X and 1.5X. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that OPT-IML generalizes more effectively across different NLP tasks compared to the current state-of-the-art.

The concept of Legitimate Peripheral Participation (LPP), a key element of social learning, is often applied to online platforms without a clear definition. This study uses the Common Interaction Context framework to analyze LPP in Scratch, a large-scale online learning platform. By examining the different types of LPP, this research uncovers new aspects of LPP and suggests that it be viewed as a complex, multi-faceted phenomenon with various forms and purposes.

The uniform electron gas is a fundamental model in condensed matter physics, used to understand the behavior of electrons in solids.  High-accuracy calculations of the uniform electron gas have validated the random phase approximation (RPA) with inclusion of exchange and correlation effects through variational perturbation theory, also known as VPT.  This method has been successfully applied to second-order perturbation theory with the two-electron-hamiltonian and Jastrow correlation factor, known as VT2JC, which has been implemented using a transcorrelated Hamiltonian.  This method has been used to obtain the electronic density, exchange-correlation energy, and energy density functional with high precision, yielding results that are in agreement with recent quantum Monte Carlo calculations.

To ensure the reliability of climate models, it is crucial to accurately quantify the uncertainty in the simulated variables. However, the uncertainty in the observation of these variables often leads to inflated estimates of the true uncertainty, a problem that arises from the limitations of the available data. In this study, we address this issue by introducing a new method that takes into account the uncertainty in the observation process. By leveraging the concept of optimal transportation, we develop a physically constrained method that incorporates the uncertainty in the observation by utilizing a Gaussian mixture model. This approach is then applied to a specific case study involving temperature and precipitation data, and the results demonstrate the effectiveness of the method in providing more accurate uncertainty estimates compared to traditional methods.

The rapid growth of data in various fields has led to the development of machine learning algorithms that can handle large datasets.  However, the high privacy risks associated with these datasets have hindered their full potential.  In response, researchers have proposed various methods to minimize these risks, such as data decomposition and privacy-enhancing techniques.  This study presents a novel, decentralized approach to data decomposition using a random tensor network, which can be applied to massive datasets stored across different locations.  By leveraging this decomposition, we can safeguard data privacy and ensure that individual data components are protected by their inherent properties.  Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach in safeguarding data privacy and the potential for further improvement in data sparsity.

We introduce SafeAPT, a novel approach to robot learning that integrates simulated training with online safe real-world deployment. This method leverages multiple policies trained in a simulated environment via evolutionary strategies, which are then combined to create a safe and efficient real-world controller. The key advantage of SafeAPT lies in its ability to achieve high real-world performance levels while minimizing the risks associated with deploying untested policies to robots. This is achieved through the strategic combination of diverse policies, allowing SafeAPT to effectively mitigate potential safety concerns during real-world deployment. Our experiments on a real-world navigation task demonstrate SafeAPT's ability to achieve high real-world performance levels while ensuring a safe and controlled approach.

The study of jet physics in radio galaxies and blazars has been a long-standing
focus in research, with a significant amount of data collected over the years.
In this review, we examine the key findings from observational studies that
have greatly advanced our understanding of jet physics, particularly in terms of
the jet's connection to its surroundings. The current understanding of jet evolution
is that it is primarily influenced by interactions between the jet and its host
environment, with a significant amount of evidence supporting this theory.
The jet's interaction with its surroundings is thought to be responsible for a
variety of phenomena observed in radio galaxies and blazars, including the
formation of radio lobes, jet precession, and the presence of jet breakouts.
The study of jet breakout has been particularly influential in this field, with a
significant amount of data collected through high-resolution imaging and
spectroscopy. The presence of jet breakout has been confirmed in a number of
systems, with a significant impact on our understanding of jet physics.
The study of jet breakout has revealed a number of key features, including the
presence of bright, jet-related features in the galaxy's central region, as well
as the presence of jet-related outbursts in the galaxy's outer regions.
The study of jet breakout has also revealed a number of key features in terms of
the jet's connection to its surroundings, including the presence of jet-related
features in the galaxy's central region, as well

This research focuses on estimating a time-inconsistent model of a time-varying nature, with a multi-dimensional response and various covariates, under the assumption that observations are sequentially available over time. A novel estimation approach is proposed, with a multi-stage framework that incorporates a weighted sieve basis adapted to the current time point to handle the complexities of time-inconsistent utility. The proposed estimator is shown to be asymptotically equivalent to a traditional sieve maximum likelihood estimator, with a rate of convergence of $n^{1/2}$. Furthermore, a modified sieve estimator is developed to accommodate the complexities of a time-varying model, with a rate of convergence of $n^{-1/4}$, and the asymptotic distribution of the modified estimator is derived. The proposed estimators are shown to be consistent and asymptotically equivalent to a traditional sieve estimator, with a multi-dimensional sample path of utility function. The efficacy of the proposed estimators is demonstrated through a Monte Carlo simulation and a real-world application using US inflation data.

The proliferation of offensive language on social media has led to a pressing need for reliable methods to identify and counter such language. This study presents a comprehensive comparison of cutting-edge neural approaches to detecting and classifying offensive content. Our investigation encompasses a range of neural network designs, including the use of pre-trained language models, multiple neural network architectures, and advanced training techniques. Furthermore, we conduct an in-depth analysis of the effectiveness of various feature extraction methods and pre-training approaches. Our findings demonstrate that a carefully optimized combination of these methods can significantly enhance the performance of state-of-the-art neural models in detecting offensive language.

The study of functional brain connectivity, a measure of brain activity relationships, is a key area of research in neuroscience. Current methods for analyzing functional connectivity, such as graph analysis, are often based on arbitrary definitions of connectivity metrics. In contrast, this study proposes a novel, data-driven approach to discovering functional connectivity patterns directly from brain activity recordings. This method uses a neural network to identify the most relevant connections between brain regions and represents the brain as a network of weighted interactions. Through this approach, we were able to uncover distinct connectivity patterns in the brain's default mode network in individuals with autism spectrum disorder compared to healthy individuals, providing new insights into the neural mechanisms of this disorder.

This paper develops a detailed analysis of Nesterov's accelerated gradient method, incorporating noise from stochastic gradients. Building on the connection between gradient descent and dissipativity, a comprehensive framework is established to provide improved estimates of the method's convergence properties. The framework is applied to both convex and non-smooth cases, providing significant advancements in our understanding of Nesterov's accelerated gradient descent. The results are further extended to a more versatile algorithm, yielding novel insights into the behavior of this novel approach.

This study presents a novel approach to deriving boundary conditions for implicit-explicit Runge-Kutta methods when applied to hyperbolic systems with viscous and vorticity terms, utilizing numerical fluxes from finite volume methods. The research also examines the stability of implicit-explicit Runge-Kutta methods when applied to hyperbolic systems with source terms, and provides a condition for numerical stability that depends on the maximum eigenvalue of the source term matrix and the maximum eigenvalue of the Runge-Kutta matrix.

The absorption of light in thin layers can be enhanced by adding a reflective surface, 
but this often results in unwanted light being scattered in directions that don't 
contribute to the desired effect. Our study shows that this issue can be resolved 
by using a 3D photonic band gap design for the reflective surface, enabling nearly 
all reflected light to be concentrated into the layer, even at very thin thicknesses. 
Furthermore, our research reveals that this technique is highly versatile and 
effective across a wide range of layer thicknesses and wavelengths, even at very low 
thicknesses in relation to the wavelength in question.

This paper introduces a novel approach to artificial reasoning by integrating credal valuation networks with plausibility distributions through a max-min message passing method. The proposed method's effectiveness is illustrated through its application in a classification task, where a Bayesian network is used to calculate the conditional probability of a particular class given a set of features. However, when the training data is limited and the features are independent, the use of a Bayesian network is inefficient and results in unnecessary computational costs. To address this issue, the paper proposes the use of credval networks, which can calculate the expected probability of a particular class by taking into account the probabilities of features and the conditional probability of a particular class given features. By applying the max-min method to credval networks, the proposed approach is able to calculate the expected probability of a particular class and achieve a high accuracy of 90% in classification, while also reducing the computational costs compared to the original Bayesian network.

The recent introduction of metric learning in top-K recommendation has yielded promising results. However, existing methods are limited in their ability to effectively leverage similarity data, and often rely on heuristic-based assumptions. This research presents a novel method, Probabilistic Metric Training with Adaptive Margin (PMT-AM), which utilizes a probabilistic metric space to model user-item pairs and incorporates margin into the loss function in a flexible manner. By applying adaptive margin to the loss function, PMT-AM can adapt to varying levels of similarity data, and has been shown to outperform existing methods on multiple real-world datasets.

The concept of non-Markovianity is commonly associated with specific properties of the dynamics of a quantum system, but it can also be applied to the dynamics of an entire quantum channel over time. In this context, a channel is considered non-Markovian at time $t$ if there exists a subchannel with a positive, non-zero trace that diverges as the channel's input approaches a specific state at that time.  A universal, time-independent criterion for determining non-Markovianity has been derived, applicable to all non-identity channels. Furthermore, a time-dependent criterion for a specific subset of non-identity channels has been formulated and demonstrated to be applicable.  These results were used to analyze the non-Markovian behavior of various specific channels, including the anti-unitary channel, the depolarizing channel, and the amplitude-damping channel.

Machine learning models are often plagued by errors, which can be particularly problematic in high-stakes applications. Rather than solely relying on post-decision fact-checking, we propose an active learning strategy that anticipates potential errors in the training data. By identifying these errors through counterfactual reasoning, selecting related examples for re-labelling, and iteratively refining the model, we can minimize future errors. Our approach is evaluated on a range of datasets and real-world datasets, and the results indicate a significant reduction in errors when employing this strategy.

The integration of autonomous robots in human environments is becoming increasingly prevalent, necessitating the development of robots that can effectively interact with their surroundings. To achieve this, robots must be equipped with the ability to navigate and understand complex, dynamic environments, including various objects and structures. To facilitate the creation of such environments, we introduce RoSmEEry, a platform that allows for the creation of realistic, simulated surroundings for robots to navigate and evaluate their performance. RoSmEEry's capabilities include the ability to import and integrate real-world environments into simulations, enabling the testing and evaluation of robots in highly realistic scenarios. We demonstrate the utility of RoSmEEry through a case study, utilizing it to create a simulated replica of a real-world office environment and evaluate the performance of a semantic mapping algorithm. The results show that RoSmEEry can generate highly realistic simulations, resulting in both quantitative and qualitative insights into the performance of robots in various scenarios.

Rikudo is a popular Japanese puzzle that involves rearranging hexagonal pieces into a specific pattern. Given a set of hexagons and a pre-existing configuration, the goal is to determine if a certain sequence of moves can transform a given hexagon into another within the existing layout. By establishing that Rikudo is equivalent to the Hamilton Path problem on graphs, and by demonstrating that Rikudo is indeed NP-hard, it can be concluded that Rikudo is also NP-hard. Furthermore, the paper also explores the parameterized complexity of Rikudo, examining the cases of bounded vertex degrees, vertex and/or edge removals, and the number of forbidden vertices.

Optimal transport has gained significant attention in multiple fields due to its ability to quantify distances between probability distributions. This leads to its potential use in a wide range of applications, including machine learning and data integration. However, calculating optimal transport distances often proves challenging due to the complexity of the underlying cost and transportation matrices. In this paper, we explore the feasibility of utilizing the fast multipole method to efficiently compute the optimal transport solution for large-scale data sets. This involves implementing the fast multipole method in both Euclidean and kernel-based settings, along with an in-depth analysis of its potential for performance enhancement. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of the method in significantly reducing computational time, thus enabling the efficient computation of optimal transport solutions for large-scale data sets.

Ramanujan's paper from 1911 contains modular identities that are closely related to group characters of the Hecke group. In this study, we use an approach developed by Evans and McKay to derive Ramanujan's modular identities from an equation that includes Hecke group character values. This study also explores the relationship between the fundamental domain of the Hecke group and partition functions.

We have obtained high-resolution R~20,000 Hubble Space Telescope F160W quasar images through Keck spectroscopy in seven out of eight lensing systems, which were observed at a range of redshifts between 0.2 and 2.3. Utilizing the multi-object spectrograph, we analyzed the spectra of the images to determine the redshifts of the lensing galaxies. These findings were then compared to the redshifts of the quasars, which were previously determined through various methods, to determine the precise redshifts of the lensing galaxies. Our results show that the lensing galaxy in one system exhibits a velocity anomaly, whereas the remaining systems display consistent velocity ratios between the lens and the quasar. Our findings also provide new lensing galaxy redshifts for seven quasars, including two that were previously unobserved. These discoveries are expected to improve the accuracy of the lensing data used in cosmological constraints.

This study focuses on resolving the $q$-fractional differential equation through the use of Riemann-Liouville fractional integrals that are in the same left-capped kernel, but with distinct order constants. Specifically, it addresses the equation $$\mathcal{I}^p_xA(x,y)f(x)=\lambda y^{-\gamma}f(x)$$ where the kernel $A(x,y)$ is defined as $A(x,y)=\frac{1}{q^x-1}\frac{\partial}{\partial x}[y^{p-q^x}f(x+\beta q^x)]$, and $\lambda$ is a constant. The solution to this equation is expressed in terms of the $q$-fractional integral of an unknown function $f(x)$, and is further analyzed using the existence and uniqueness theorems. Additionally, several results are derived for the boundedness and continuous solutions of the equation, and illustrative examples are presented to validate the proposed approach.

The emergence of a significant phonon Hall effect in bismuth and graphite, 
resulting in substantial phonon Hall conductivity, has garnered considerable 
attention. In this study, we delve into the topological characteristics of the 
phonon band structure in graphene-like materials using the Dirac Hamiltonian. 
Through the Weyl node decomposition of phonon band inversions, we demonstrate 
that the phonon Hall effect can be attributed to the phonon Weyl points and 
edges. Furthermore, we observe that the phonon Hall effect is primarily driven by 
the phonon Weyl points' non-zero Berry curvature, resulting in high mobility 
and conductivity.

This research introduces a novel approach to spatially resolved Raman imaging, leveraging the Nod and Shuffle Infrared Spectrometer to record Raman spectra from various regions of a sample. By employing SER SERS, this method excites the sample with two distinct laser wavelengths and captures Raman spectra using two separate detectors. We applied this technique to a 10 micron thick section of a tobacco leaf, which was mounted in a 1mm thick sapphire substrate, by activating Raman signals with 785nm and 1064nm lasers. The resulting data was analyzed using the Nod and Shuffle algorithm, which allowed us to generate a Raman map of the sample. The map revealed a clear distinction between the cuticle and cell wall regions, as well as the cuticle thickness variations across different cell walls within the same leaf.

The research focuses on establishing matrix versions of Fej\'{e}r and Levin-St\v{c}kin inequalities for specific types of matrices. It includes a particular case related to positive self-adjoint operators in a Hilbert space.

We examine the mean null energy condition for the event horizon of four/ five-dimensional black holes that undergo evaporation. Due to the asymmetry introduced by the non-isotropic evaporation process, the mean energy density becomes location-dependent on the horizon. A thorough analysis of the mean null energy condition reveals that its violation occurs near the future and past event horizons simultaneously. Notably, this condition holds near the past event horizon, yet it is violated near the future event horizon, contrasting with the classic black hole scenario. Furthermore, this location-dependent violation of the mean null energy condition suggests a distinct, evanescent black hole scenario that diverges from the classic black hole behavior.

In this paper, we examine the properties of conformal field theories in relation to their associated Lie algebras, with a focus on dimensions that are rational in the sense of the theory. We derive a method for calculating dimensions involving an infinite series of conformal dimensions, present a computational tool for evaluating these dimensions, and provide examples of dimensions that are rational in specific cases.

The rapid expansion of the Internet of Things (IoT) has led to a significant increase in the number of connected devices, resulting in a growing need for robust cybersecurity measures for IoT-based systems. Despite the importance of formal cybersecurity testing, there is a lack of standardized methodologies in this area. To bridge this gap, we propose a new model for cybersecurity testing, specifically designed for industrial control systems (ICSs), which provides a framework for evaluating and improving the effectiveness of cybersecurity testing for ICSs.

In complex, dynamic environments, multiple agents must make informed decisions to achieve a coordinated goal, but their individual actions can be influenced by other agents' decisions, creating a need for coordination. This coordination problem is further complicated by the need for agents to consider the impact of other agents' actions on their own decision-making processes. To address this challenge, we present a new approach to multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) called Greedy-based Worth Representation (GWR) that enables agents to evaluate the contributions of their fellow agents to the overall decision-making process. By using a greedy algorithm to calculate the value of individual agents, the proposed method allows agents to make more informed decisions, leading to improved decision quality and increased coordination. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of GWR in improving decision-making outcomes, particularly in scenarios with limited communication among agents.

This research investigates the stereotypical bias in pre-trained language models by developing StereoSet, a benchmark dataset consisting of 12,000 high-confidence statements that conform to 36 common stereotypes about women and older individuals. We examine the prevalence of stereotypical bias in six prominent models, including GPT-2, GPT-3, RoBERTa, XLM-R, DistilBERT, and BERT-Large. We also propose a framework for StereoSet that leverages the models' language generation capabilities to uncover previously unobserved stereotypical bias. The findings reveal that all six models exhibit significant bias towards women and older individuals, with GPT-3 and XLM-R displaying particularly striking examples of this bias. Moreover, our StereoSet framework enables the identification of novel stereotypical statements that were not present in existing datasets, such as those related to older individuals.

The optimization of power system operations is complicated by the presence of uncertainties. In our research, we address the problem of optimizing electrical tilt control for renewable energy sources, such as wind and solar power, despite uncertainty in tilt policy. To tackle this issue, we develop a novel off-policy reinforcement learning method that enables efficient learning under uncertain conditions. The approach is tested on a realistic model of the Eastern Seaboard network in Australia, where we aim to minimize the loss of power transmission by learning from historical data. The results demonstrate that our method outperforms a baseline policy by a significant margin, with a 20% reduction in loss of power transmission.

A combination of existing LHCb results on the CKM angle $\gamma$ from various $B$-meson decays is provided, along with an estimate of systematics and correlated errors. An updated determination of $\gamma$ is made by incorporating all six decays, yielding a value of $\gamma = (102^{+44}{}_{-41})^\circ$. This combination is also accompanied by a correlation coefficient of $0.61$ between the values of $\gamma$ derived from $B^0 \rightarrow \phi\pi^0$ and $B^0 \rightarrow \phi\pi^+$ decays.

This paper delves into the geometric properties of a specific type of ellipsoid, where the ratio of its semi-axes is expressed through a formula involving the cosine of a given angle, yielding a result that's not as straightforward as one might expect. By employing an approach that's distinct from, yet related to, the traditional method of coordinate transformation, we explore the complex symmetries of this particular ellipsoid. Ultimately, our analysis leads to a notable identity involving the cosine of a square root index of a given number. Notably, this investigation serves as an illustration of how geometric attributes of an object can be accessed through the study of its complex symmetries.

A recent study in the United Kingdom on a diverse group of participants found that, when given the option to earn money, many people are willing to sell personal data online. A survey conducted as part of the research revealed that, when given a substantial financial incentive, both men and women are equally likely to participate in the market. However, men tend to be more aggressive in setting their prices compared to women, particularly when it comes to more sensitive information such as GPS data and browsing history. Additionally, individuals from lower socio-economic backgrounds were found to be more willing to compete in the market, while women and those with lower levels of educational attainment were more likely to prefer setting higher prices for more sensitive data. These findings have significant implications for the development of a legitimate personal data market, particularly in terms of ensuring that a level playing field exists among different market participants.

In the context of non-binary code detection, researchers have explored various methods such as maximum likelihood and sphere decoding to address the challenge. These existing solutions rely on specific architectures and are not directly applicable to non-standard signaling formats. This paper proposes a universal framework for detecting any standard or non-standard signaling format, leveraging the potential of list sphere decoding and deep learning to achieve this goal. A deep neural network is incorporated to efficiently search for valid symbols within a specified error radius, thereby significantly reducing computational complexity compared to traditional list sphere decoding. The proposed method is particularly beneficial in scenarios involving standard signaling formats and is thus suitable for implementation in communication systems. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of this approach, showcasing its potential to achieve up to 80% reduction in computational complexity while maintaining a 1.5 dB performance advantage over traditional methods.

We establish that every effect algebra E with a certain operator and two specific properties can be ordered in such a way that it resembles a certain type of algebra, and we show that this ordering is equivalent to a certain finite property. We then use this ordering to show that the set of states in E forms a particular type of topological space, and we relate this topology to a certain space involving real numbers. Additionally, we prove that a certain type of ideal in E is related to a certain space involving real numbers, and we show that this space is equivalent to a certain space involving real numbers, and we relate it to a certain type of algebra involving subspaces of real numbers.

Recent advancements in deep learning have led to the development of highly accurate models, but these models often rely on chance and are susceptible to manipulation. To mitigate these issues, researchers have proposed various regularization techniques, with the primary goal of reducing overfitting and improving model robustness. To address these concerns, this paper introduces a novel data augmentation strategy called SaliencyMix, which aims to enhance the generalizability of deep learning models. By generating mixed images, SaliencyMix leverages saliency maps to identify the most informative image regions, thereby improving model performance on natural images. Our experiments demonstrate the efficacy of SaliencyMix, which outperforms existing data augmentation strategies, including MixUp and CutMix, on a range of benchmark datasets, including CIFAR-10/100, SVHN, and ImageNet.

We investigate certain types of infinite-dimensional $\operatorname{GL}(2,\mathbb{R})$ Hecke algebras, denoted as $\mathcal{H}^\pi$, by focusing on their unitary representations and character formulas. We introduce a novel concept, the $\operatorname{GL}(2,\mathbb{R})$-block, which encompasses a set of irreducible representations sharing a common trace. This $\operatorname{GL}(2,\mathbb{R})$-block framework allows us to establish a correspondence with the $p$-adic $\operatorname{GL}(2,\mathbb{F}_p)$-block framework, thereby providing an analogue of the Lusztig correspondence in the infinite-dimensional setting.

A new, four-dimensional theory known as Altered (Horndeski) gravity has been proposed to address various cosmological anomalies, yet it requires further testing to confirm its validity. This study explores a novel method to test this theory using a combination of data from two sources: the intrinsic galaxy alignments and cosmic shear from a specific redshift range. This approach involves developing a novel framework to predict how the theory affects the gravitational lensing of distant galaxies, which can be observed through their elliptical shapes. This method provides a new way to constrain the theory's parameters, specifically the $c_4$ parameter, resulting in a 3-sigma limit of $-1.6 \pm 0.7 \times 10^{-5}$. The study also demonstrates that the combination of data from intrinsic galaxy alignments and cosmic shear can be used to test the theory's predictions more effectively than using either data set alone.

In this research, we have investigated the complex flow behavior of soft, porous particles by analyzing the relationship between stress and rate of strain under steady shear conditions. Our findings reveal a unique characteristic of particle fluidity that is influenced by the local density of the surrounding fluid, resulting in a non-monotonic behavior with respect to shear rate. This non-monotonic behavior is a direct consequence of the interplay between the particles' softness and their interparticle forces, leading to a significant change in the fluid's viscosity at a critical shear rate. Our study also explores the effects of varying parameters such as particle size, interparticle energy, and fluid density on this non-Newtonian behavior.

A novel method is proposed that combines experimental data and classical molecular dynamics simulations. This method, known as the 'data-informed simulation', is capable of accurately representing the temperature at which gold atoms begin to melt within 5 nanometers and above in a nanoscale spherical particle. This technique is based on matching the thermal properties observed in heat capacity experiments to a simulated system. This method is also applicable to other materials and in scenarios where heat is transferred through a solid that contains imperfections. This technique is also shown to be useful in determining the temperature at which atoms melt within a solid that contains voids.

This is the initial component of a two-part study focusing on the general framework for proving splitting theorems and bifurcations in the context of nonlinear operators with potential, which encompasses both selfadjoint and non-selfadjoint elliptic and parabolic differential operators. Ultimately, the final segment of this series will apply these concepts to investigate a broad class of nonlinear operators arising from perturbed operators with complex boundary conditions. The current part primarily concentrates on the creation of a theoretical framework, which includes a novel approach to non-selfadjoint elliptic differential operators.

The concept of taste tasting panels is widely used in the food industry to assess the taste of products, often involving a panel of individuals who blindly taste various foods and provide feedback on their flavors. Interestingly, taste panelists' ratings of the same food consistently align and correlate with the expertly crafted flavor profiles created by professional mixologists. Notably, these flavor profiles can be represented as a four-dimensional space, where each axis corresponds to different taste components. Building on this idea, we've developed a method to embed this four-dimensional space into a three-dimensional one, leveraging the properties of Riemannian manifolds. Our approach is based on the work of Lovett, who demonstrated that any four-dimensional space can be mapped to a three-dimensional one. We've applied our method to real taste panel data, creating a three-dimensional space that accurately captures the taste of various foods.
We derive new identities for (h,q)-Genocchi numbers and polynomials within the p-adic integer domain by employing the p-adic Euler-Maclaurin formula, and also incorporate the beta function.

In this research, we address the issue of estimating long-term treatment effects in survival data, specifically in scenarios where the time of death is subject to restrictions due to censoring. Our approach involves developing a reinforcement learning method that utilizes the principal strata framework to account for unobservable confounding factors. The method incorporates a novel action-dependent survival model, allowing us to directly analyze the impact of treatments on survival rates. Furthermore, we propose a cost function that incorporates treatment effects and survival rates, enabling the maximization of long-term outcomes through policy optimization. Our model allows for the direct calculation of causal effects on survival rates and the identification of treatment effects on specific segments of the population. Our findings demonstrate the superiority of the proposed method over existing approaches in both simulated and real-world datasets.

In case-control studies, researchers investigate the link between a specific exposure and a disease by comparing groups of individuals with and without the disease who were exposed and unexposed. However, researchers often face challenges in analyzing such studies because they typically rely on data from sources that are already categorized, making it difficult to balance the groups. To address this issue, researchers often use stratification, but this method can be flawed due to the risk of imbalance within strata. To mitigate this problem, researchers have developed a new method that incorporates the memory bias problem into a framework that allows for the analysis of data from groups that are not perfectly balanced. This approach involves using a statistical test that accounts for potential biases in the data, allowing researchers to analyze the impact of exposures on disease risk. To demonstrate the effectiveness of this method, researchers have applied it to a study of the relationship between a specific exposure and a disease in a general practice database.

Generative models can be trained in two distinct ways: either by optimizing a lower bound on the model evidence, or by maximizing the likelihood of the training data. The former approach is more efficient, but only applicable to supervised training scenarios. The latter method, on the other hand, can handle unsupervised training, albeit at a higher computational cost due to the need to sample from the model. We have developed a novel, invertible neural network architecture that allows for exact maximum likelihood training of generative autoencoders. Our method is comparable in efficiency to the more efficient evidence lower bound approach, yet offers the advantage of being trainable in both supervised and unsupervised settings. We have demonstrated the effectiveness of our method in a variety of applications, including image and text generation, and achieved state-of-the-art results in image and text modeling.

The concept of "smart cities" has become a prominent goal for urban planners and government officials, enabling them to make informed decisions through a deeper understanding of their citizens' needs. By leveraging cutting-edge data mining and machine learning techniques, smart city initiatives can be bolstered and residents' quality of life improved. However, the vast amounts of data generated require sophisticated analysis to unlock valuable insights. Our research focuses on developing a set of innovative data mining algorithms that can be applied to smart city data, specifically related to demographic attributes. These algorithms are designed to be visually engaging, allowing stakeholders to easily explore and interpret the results. Our approach is illustrated through a case study of the city of Graz, Austria, and we demonstrate how our methods can be applied to other smart city projects.

This study explores the numerical solution of two classes of linear systems derived from the HDG-P0 method for the reaction-diffusion equation and the generalized Stokes equations. The reaction-diffusion equation is solved using a multi-field approach, while the generalized Stokes equations are solved using a pressure-based approach. To optimize the HDG-P0 method for both problems, we develop an algebraic multi-level preconditioning strategy that leverages optimized coarse spaces and matrix-based smoothing to achieve robustness. The effectiveness of our approach is demonstrated through a comprehensive numerical investigation of its performance for both problems.

Missing data in scientific studies can lead to biased results. To address this, we propose a new method for evaluating the sensitivity of analysis to these missing data, which is based on the E-value. Our approach, which is grounded in the principles of missing data analysis, involves analyzing the effect of the data analysis procedure on the estimated associations. By considering the impact of data analysis on associations and the probability of false alarms, we can evaluate the reliability of associations and the likelihood of false discoveries. To demonstrate the effectiveness of this method, we conducted a simulation study and applied it to a real-world dataset related to the risk of lung cancer.

In crossover trials where multiple treatment periods are employed, missing data can compromise the efficacy of treatment period analyses. To address this challenge, a probability-based approach is developed to estimate treatment effects while accounting for missing data. This approach is applied to a multivariate crossover trial where subjects receive multiple treatments and multiple dosage forms, with the analysis conducted using the mixed treatment effects model. Treatment periods with a single period of varying doses are treated as separate single-period studies, while 3 and 4 period designs are treated as repeated study sequences. To estimate missing data, a two-stage approach is used, with the first stage involving the analysis of observed data and the second stage involving the imputation of missing data based on a linear mixed effects model. Treatment effects are estimated using the EM algorithm, with the analysis focusing on the treatment by sequence interaction effect. To validate the approach, a simulation study is conducted to assess its performance across various scenarios of missing data. This approach is then applied to a real-world clinical trial data set.

We define and analyze the properties of weak monoidal frameworks on categories, which provide a more general framework for studying certain geometric objects called SASS associahedra, allowing for their classification in various categories of geometric objects.

The growing demand for cloud services and emerging applications has led to an increase in memory access intensity, prompting the need for more efficient memory access.  In order to optimize memory access, we introduce a new framework called CODIC, which allows for the customization of memory access functionality within the memory itself.  CODIC achieves this through the implementation of a hardware module that inserts a small set of bits into DRAM address lines, effectively enabling the modification of memory access behavior.  By utilizing a hardware-software co-design approach, CODIC can be integrated with existing DRAM chips and processors without requiring extensive modifications.  Our framework is highly flexible and can be used to implement a wide range of memory access optimizations, including those that cannot be achieved through traditional means such as operating system and compiler optimizations.  As a result, CODIC can significantly improve the performance of memory-intensive applications, including graph processing and in-memory databases, by up to 2.5X and 1.5X respectively, with minimal added cost.

This paper is the second installment in a series, and it delves into how functional programming can be utilized in network management and resource allocation. By leveraging this paradigm, we can more effectively monitor and manage network resources, moving beyond traditional resource management to a more comprehensive approach that prioritizes network quality and service delivery. Furthermore, this paper will explore the implications of functional programming on network evolution, and how it can inform the design of future networks.

In a physical implementation of the toric code, where each face of a regular lattice corresponds to a logical qubit, we investigate the feasibility of performing a variety of operations on each face. We examine the costs associated with these operations and consider how to optimize them to achieve specific gates. Our analysis reveals that, while certain operations on each face are sufficient to implement any unitary transformation in the two-dimensional space, those necessary for multi-qubit operations are significantly more resource-intensive compared to their one-qubit counterparts.

A task control system is a critical component in an observatory, enabling the execution of complex scientific projects. This type of system is responsible for allocating resources, such as telescope time, to fulfill the demands of these projects. In the context of large astronomical observatories, task control systems must be highly scalable, efficient, and reliable. To address this need, the OPUS system was developed. OPUS is based on Open Grid Services, a service-oriented architecture that allows for seamless integration with observatory assets. This results in a robust and reliable system for managing tasks. Additionally, the use of Open Planning Services and Web Services protocols ensures interoperability with other systems, making OPUS a versatile solution. As a result, the OPUS system has been successfully deployed in various astronomical facilities, including the ALMA telescope and the VISTA telescope at the ESO Paranal Observatory.

A novel approach to educational learning is proposed, focusing on interactive game-driven learning through digital games, specifically for students of advanced wireless networks. The game-driven learning method is demonstrated to be effective in teaching students of upper-level Computer Science and Engineering majors in prominent technical institutions. The results indicate that game-driven learning outcomes are comparable to traditional classroom settings in educating students of complex topics in wireless networks. The method's effectiveness in teaching diverse network concepts, including Quality of Service and the Impact of Network Association on Quality of Experience, is highlighted. The results suggest that game-driven learning can be an efficient and engaging educational approach for sensitive and technical topics.

The relationship between molecular oxygen and ozone has been studied in various planetary systems, often used as a key indicator of a habitable environment. However, research suggests that atmospheric conditions on Earth and other planets are more complex, making the O2-O3 relationship less certain. To better understand this relationship, scientists have created a model that simulates atmospheric conditions on Earth and other planets, using it to analyze how changing parameters such as stellar radiation and water availability affect the balance between O2 and O3. The results show that atmospheric conditions on planets with low gravity and low water availability differ significantly from those on Earth, often resulting in higher ozone levels and lower oxygen levels. The model also suggests that atmospheric conditions on planets with higher land coverage and dryness will result in higher ozone levels and lower oxygen levels. The relationship between O2 and O3 is also influenced by the presence of greenhouse gases and ozone-depleting substances, with certain combinations leading to higher ozone levels and lower oxygen levels. The model's findings indicate that a stable and habitable environment with a strong greenhouse effect and moderate water availability is characterized by higher ozone levels and lower oxygen levels, contradicting the conventional O2-O3 relationship.

We investigate the Hofstadter model under two different scenarios: when the lattice is placed under a tilt and when the magnetic flux varies uniformly.  The Hofstadter model exhibits a series of Hofstadter bands which are characterized by the filling factor.  Near the band edges, the Hofstadter model exhibits a quantized Hall effect, similar to its two-dimensional counterpart.  In this study, we reveal that Hofstadter bands host robust surface currents that are resistant to tilts and variations in the magnetic flux.  The Hofstadter model's surface currents are analogous to the edge currents observed in quantum Hall systems, but they differ in that they are confined to the edges of the third spatial dimension.  The robust nature of these surface currents stems from the presence of a quantized Berry phase, which is a characteristic of the Hofstadter model.  The Berry phase is responsible for the invariance of these surface currents to tilts and variations in the magnetic flux.  Furthermore, we demonstrate that Hofstadter model's surface currents are robust against disorder and remain unchanged even when the Hofstadter model is perturbed with random site energies.  The robust Hofstadter model is a promising candidate for the development of new quantum technologies, including high-performance quantum electronics and advanced quantum information processing systems.

Recent advancements in Multilingual Neural Machine Translation (NMT) have led to significant improvements in translating medical texts across languages. However, these models often struggle when applied to domain-specific texts due to the lack of domain-specific training data. To overcome this, we propose a hybrid approach that combines multilingual NMT with additional training in a target domain. Experimental results on translating medical texts between four languages demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach, which outperforms a purely multilingual model by a substantial margin, achieving improvements of up to 11.2 BLEU points in a target language.

A theoretical investigation into the influence of electrostatic altered-ion-acoustic waves (AIAWs) in a multi-ionic plasma with positively charged dust particles has been conducted, accounting for ion temperature and nonthermal electron influences. The study revealed that the properties of AIAWs, including their propagation direction and soliton and shock wave properties, are significantly altered by the presence of dust, temperature, and nonthermal electrons. A detailed analysis of the parameter space showed that the waves' properties can be controlled by adjusting these parameters. Furthermore, it was found that the waves' speed and their ability to exist in a particular region of the parameter space depend on the density ratio of the plasma components. The study also demonstrated that the presence of dust particles can lead to the formation of AIAWs with increased speed and stiffer soliton and shock wave profiles, which can be experimentally or directly observed using a variety of plasma devices.

Recent advancements in unsupervised pre-training have led to significant improvements in cross-lingual and multi-lingual natural language processing tasks. Nevertheless, the majority of these advancements have been confined to the analysis of individual sentences. This study introduces a novel pre-training method that integrates contextual information into sentence representation, thereby enhancing the performance in downstream tasks. The proposed approach is applied to the cross-lingual compact retrieval task, where it is compared to the current state-of-the-art models. The results demonstrate that the new method achieves comparable performance while utilizing a reduced number of parameters, and its effectiveness is further validated through the analysis of its cross-modal and cross-lingual embeddings.

Multimodal learning models have achieved significant success in various tasks, yet their performance is often hindered by inconsistent modal distributions. This issue arises due to the disparity in data availability among different tasks, causing some modalities to be overrepresented while others are underrepresented. To address this problem, we present a novel method that adjusts modal distributions to match the most common modality per sample, thereby mitigating the negative effects of distributional imbalance. This approach is implemented in a prototypical sampling framework, where prototypes are generated from the most frequent modality for each task. Experimental results on multiple datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our method, especially in scenarios with extreme distributional imbalances.

In the context of vector models for non-equilibrium dynamics, we develop a transport theory that incorporates the engagement of vector kinematics. This engagement enables the derivation of kinetic equations that incorporate not just bosonic and fermionic degrees of freedom, but also those related to the engagement itself. Our theory is applied to a non-equilibrium process, such as the evolution of a thermal state through a massless vector field. By solving the kinetic equation, we obtain a general expression for the two-point function's late-time dependence, from which we determine the scaling exponents and identify the conditions under which these exponents vary.

This study presents a novel approach to spoken command recognition, leveraging a deep neural network model that combines a tensor-train network with a 1D convolutional neural network. In contrast to traditional methods, our model employs a hidden state that encodes temporal and spatial information, thereby facilitating the learning of temporal dependencies. We employed a pre-trained model based on the ResNet-50 architecture to obtain spatially invariant features, which were subsequently used as input to our proposed network. Experimental results on the FLIC+ dataset demonstrate the efficacy of our model, achieving state-of-the-art performance with a word error rate of 0.115, outperforming conventional sequence classification models.

The theory of quantum jumps provides a clear visual representation of quantum dynamics, making it easier to understand the evolution of open quantum systems. However, it's still a challenge to develop a detailed picture of this process. To tackle this issue, researchers have created a new approach to breaking down quantum dynamics into step-by-step quantum jumps. This method involves using different mathematical models to describe quantum systems and then comparing the resulting trajectories. The approach was successfully applied to a specific type of optical cavity model, revealing new insights into its behavior under different conditions.

The incorporation of plasmonic nanoparticles into thin-film crystalline silicon materials has been found to boost their absorption capabilities, thereby increasing energy conversion efficiency. Despite the numerous studies on metal nanostructures, research on aluminum (Al) remains relatively underexplored. This study delves into the optical effects of cylindrical and pyramidal Al nanostructures atop c-Si thin-film solar cells. Using finite-difference time-domain (FDTD) simulations, we investigate the impact of these aluminum nanostructures on absorption in c-Si solar cells, considering various dimensions and layer configurations. Our findings indicate that pyramidal aluminum nanoparticles outperform cylindrical ones in absorption enhancement, with the pyramidal shape exhibiting a higher absorption rate. The optimal dimensions for both shapes are identified, with the pyramidal shape showing a higher absorption rate at a particular size. The results also reveal that incorporating these aluminum nanoparticles into solar cells can increase absorption by as much as 1.5 times, with the pyramidal shape performing better. The study demonstrates that both shapes can enhance absorption in c-Si solar cells, with the pyramidal shape offering superior performance.

The concept of logics employing existential quantification and allowing for the representation of finite structures through means such as bounded expansion or solution lengths has been explored in the past. Building on the previous work of Feferman and Sanchis, as well as Sgandurella and Szczerba, we investigate the addition of an existential choice operator to second-order logic, which we consider to be the most basic form of such logics.
